title: Turning a 2017 MacBook Pro into a Home fnOS NAS
summary: A hands-on log of building a home fnOS NAS on a spare 2017 MacBook Pro — install pitfalls, Ventoy boot, plus useful patterns for cloud-drive mounts and projector movie nights.
markdown:
![image]()

## Why a MacBook as a NAS

We had a 2017 MacBook Pro sitting unused for a long time. Honestly, it still has decent horsepower — just not enough to stay as a daily driver. Rather than let it collect dust, better to put the leftover life to work.

I had been looking at NAS setups and wondered whether this old Mac could be the machine. Compared with buying a ready-made NAS or building a dedicated box, reusing what you already own is the cheapest way to fail: the hardware is there; if you break it, no tears.

For the OS I landed on fnOS (Feiniu). Two reasons mainly:

- Modern UI, easy to learn (I did not want a pure command-line grind)
- Strong support for Chinese cloud drives (Baidu Netdisk, Aliyun Drive, and friends can all mount)

### 2. Prep before install

Hardware I gathered first:

- MacBook Pro 2017 (the star of the show)
- USB-C Ethernet adapter (stable network matters)
- One 8GB USB stick (for the installer)
- One 10TB drive (for data)

With hardware ready I started searching. Most people online run a VM path — UTM on macOS, then fnOS inside the VM.

I did not want that layer. A VM always costs performance and feel. My idea: install fnOS on the MacBook the way you install Linux — bare metal.

With that goal, attempt one began.

### 3. First install: the pit

Following the official fnOS guide I did this:

1. Downloaded the fnOS system image
1. Wrote it to the USB stick with Etcher
1. Rebooted the MacBook, held Option for the boot picker
1. Booted from USB and finished the installer wizard

Install itself was smooth — about 30 minutes. Success message, happy me, unplugged the stick, rebooted.

Then… black screen.

After boot, pure black, nothing on the display. I thought the boot entry was wrong, tried again, same result. BIOS/EFI settings showed the system was installed — it just would not start.

After half a day of thrashing I realized the problem was bootstrapping. fnOS was on disk, but the MacBook boot chain could not launch it cleanly.

### 4. The fix that worked: Ventoy

Right when I was about to give up, I saw someone mention Ventoy.

![image]()

In short, Ventoy is a multi-boot USB tool: drop several ISOs on one stick and pick at boot. More importantly, it can not only install systems — it can also boot systems that are already installed.

That was exactly my problem. The OS was installed; only boot failed. So boot it with Ventoy.

### Steps

1. Download Ventoy (https://www.ventoy.net)
1. Rebuild the USB stick with Ventoy (this formats the stick)
1. Copy the fnOS image file onto the stick as a normal file
1. Plug in the stick and reboot the MacBook
1. In the Ventoy menu, choose the fnOS system

This time it worked.

The system started and opened the fnOS admin UI. Booting still needs the USB stick every time — but it runs. Stage win.

### 5. First impressions: a clean UI

First reaction after logging in: the interface is genuinely fresh.

Compared with classic NAS UIs, fnOS looks modern — closer to a cloud admin console. Comfortable colors, clear icons, intuitive flows.

The home screen shows live status:

- CPU and memory use
- Network traffic (up/down)
- Storage read/write
- Uptime

My MacBook runs fnOS without stress — CPU often around 45%, about 5.2GB RAM used, smooth overall.

![image]()

### 6. Features that won me over

After living with it a while, a few features stood out.

### 1. Two-way backup

Genuinely useful. It supports:

- **Local → cloud**: auto-back up important NAS files to Baidu Netdisk, Aliyun Drive, etc.
- **Cloud → local**: sync cloud files down to the NAS

That is dual insurance: one copy local, one in the cloud — less fear of losing data.

### 2. Remote cloud mounts

This was the biggest surprise. fnOS can mount major Chinese cloud drives directly. I mounted three:

![image]()

- Baidu Netdisk (SVIP, 100GB)
- Aliyun Drive (8.73TB)
- Quark Drive (6TB)

Once mounted they behave like local disks. Better still, you can move files between clouds without download-then-upload through your laptop.

Speed-wise, Quark is clearly faster. Upload and download both stay stable and nearly fill my bandwidth. Baidu, even on SVIP, still feels a step behind.

### 3. Photos

Built-in photo library auto-organizes phone pictures by time and place — easy to find things later.

The UI is decent too; browsing feels close to a dedicated photo app. For someone whose phone storage is always full, this is basically a must-have.

### 4. Media library

Built-in movie/TV library: drop films and shows in, auto-fetch metadata, posters, and blurbs. Looks polished.

![image]()

This matters a lot for projector nights.

Before, watching a movie meant either dumping files onto a USB stick for the projector or running HDMI to a computer. Annoying, and a stick cannot hold many Blu-ray rips.

With the fnOS media app, the projector hits the NAS library over the network. On the sofa, remote in hand, pick and play — same convenience as a streaming service.

Large Blu-ray files are fine too. 40GB or 50GB titles stream without stutter on a gigabit LAN; picture and sound stay original.

Way better than juggling USB sticks — watch whatever you want without shuttling files.

### 5. Built-in UPS (kind of)

Unexpected bonus. Building a NAS on a MacBook has an advantage people miss: the laptop battery is a free UPS.

![image]()

fnOS reads the MacBook battery cleanly. In the UI you can see:

- Power source: AC
- Remaining charge: 93%
- Connection: normal
- Shutdown rules (e.g. auto power-off below a threshold)

What does that mean? Power cuts are less scary. The system switches to battery, the NAS keeps running, writes finish, data stays safe.

On a desktop or typical NAS box you would pay hundreds (or more) for a UPS. On a MacBook it is free.

For data safety that matters. Occasional breaker trips or maintenance outages stop being a crisis. The battery can last hours — enough to wait for power or shut down cleanly.

A laptop NAS advantage you do not get from a tower. Clever, really.

### 7. Side discovery: a better Quark workflow

After a while I found a slick Quark pattern.

I used to download Blu-ray movies via torrents. Even with Thunder hanging there, speeds were miserable. A 40GB film could take a whole day.

New path:

1. Save the torrent into Quark first (Quark supports offline download)
1. Quark finishes the download in the cloud (often minutes)
1. Pull from Quark to the local NAS at full line speed

Measured:

- Before: Thunder at 100–500 KB/s — 40GB needed 10+ hours
- Now: Quark offline ~5 minutes, then NAS download fills 100 Mbps — ~1 hour for 40GB

Faster, and Quark's 6TB holds the titles I rewatch so they are always ready.

### 8. A small RAID detour

After install I planned to buy another 10TB HDD and RAID it with the existing one for redundancy.

Then I checked prices on JD — drives had gone up.

The same 10TB spinner cost hundreds more than a few months earlier. RAID is safer, but for a home NAS regular cloud backup is often enough.

So that plan is on hold until prices drop. fnOS backup already covers the safety angle for now.

### 9. Wrap-up

After all the thrashing, plenty learned:

1. **Old gear, new life**: a 2017 MacBook Pro is more than enough for a home NAS
1. **New tool**: Ventoy solved a hard problem cleanly
1. **Useful features**: cloud mounts, two-way backup, Quark download tricks
1. **Money saved**: no need to buy a finished NAS box

As of writing it has been stable for 9+ days (per screenshots) with no drama. CPU and memory look healthy; thermals are fine.

**Who is this for?**

If you also have a spare MacBook (especially ~2017 x86 models) and want a home NAS, this path is worth trying — if you:

- Do not mind tinkering (you will hit pits)
- Can live with booting from a USB stick (Ventoy)
- Want a full-featured NAS with a modern UI

**What is next**

- Keep watching long-term stability
- Expand storage or RAID when drive prices cool
- Explore fnOS Docker and deploy a few useful apps
- See if I can drop Ventoy and boot natively

Overall, worth the hassle. A idle MacBook became a capable home data center. Reusing old gear often feels better than buying something new.
